evidence_quotes.quote: We do so by examining how the central cities in the 22 largest metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) in this region are responding to potential shortfalls in their water supply.
We seek to explain why demand-reduction approaches have become important in some cities and remain unimportant in other cities, even in a region where hydrological conditions are quite similar.
To address research question 2, we used a quantitative method to understand what factors best explain the strength of demand-reduction strategies in the overall water-supply regime.
The Vanderbilt Water Conservation Index (VWCIb) is a count of the water conservation policies and programs within a city.
The variable importance plot shows the overwhelming importance of the PVI as a predictor of the VWCIb.

criterion_notes.c1: No. The study examines municipal water-supply strategies in response to drought (supply-increase projects such as pipelines, reservoirs, aquifer recharge, and desalination versus city-wide demand-reduction/conservation programs) across 22 Southwestern US cities, rather than household or community water or sanitation service access (Exclusion Criterion 7).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — the study examines institutional and governance factors, including contending institutional logics, urban growth coalitions, partisan political preferences, and municipal water conservation policies/ordinances. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: No — the study does not evaluate how a legal or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governs household or community service access; instead, the count of municipal conservation policies and programs (VWCIb) is the city-level dependent variable explained by partisan voting preferences (Cook's Partisan Voting Index), regional price parity, hydrological variables, and macro political/institutional logics.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Convergent mixed-methods empirical study combining qualitative coding of utility documents and media reports on water-policy conflicts with quantitative decision-tree and random-forest analyses across 22 MSAs/central cities.
criterion_notes.c4: No. The reported outcomes are city-level counts of adopted water conservation policies and programs (VWCIb score), inventories of planned municipal supply-increase infrastructure, and classifications of political conflicts over water-supply regimes — not household or community water service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. For the study's own research questions, the unit of analysis and sample (22 largest MSAs/central cities in the extended American Southwest), exposures (institutional logics and sociopolitical/hydrological predictors), outcomes (VWCIb score and conflict typology), and mixed-methods design are clearly specified.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English.

study_design: Convergent mixed-methods cross-sectional study (qualitative analysis of utility documents and media reports; quantitative regression tree and random forest models)
population_and_sample: Central cities in the 22 largest metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) of the extended American Southwest (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas, and Utah; n = 22 cities/MSAs)
exposure: Institutional logics (development, preservation, environmental, consumer) and city/MSA sociopolitical and hydrological factors (Cook's Partisan Voting Index, regional price parity, population, population growth, temperature, precipitation, surface-water percentage, and drought duration)
outcome: Municipal adoption of demand-reduction policies and programs measured by the Vanderbilt Water Conservation Index (VWCIb), planned supply-increase strategies, and political conflicts over water-supply strategies
rationale: Excluded under E01 (Wrong topic; see Exclusion Criterion 7, water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). Although empirical (c3 = yes), the paper investigates urban drought adaptation and why 22 Southwestern US cities adopt municipal water conservation/demand-reduction portfolios versus supply-increase infrastructure, explained by partisan voting preferences (PVI) and contending institutional logics. It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1 = no), does not test a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification (c2 = no), and reports municipal conservation policy counts (VWCIb) and political conflict typologies rather than service access outcomes (c4 = no).
